Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{1}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{1}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{1}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{E}_{1}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}:$

$$
{E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
